In shock and overcome with emotion that morning, Savile called the RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters) line and in less than an hour conservation officers arrived to remove the trap from Berta, who had failed to return home earlier this month. She said officers helped load Berta’s body into her and her family’s truck, which they brought back home to bury in their backyard. Berta was a five-year-old Maremma livestock guardian dog adopted in Alberta who Savile described as a great protector in keeping predators away and everyone safe, including their neighbour’s sheep and goats. British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. Doerkson would probably be among the first to acknowledge that his route to the premiership has been anything but typical. Of the last five B.C. premiers, three were political staffers and two were lawyers, and many MLAs start their road to the provincial legislature via local politics: the MLAs-elect for the two Kamloops ridings bordering Cariboo-Chilcotin, Peter Milobar and Ward Stamer, were first the mayors of Kamloops and Barriere respectively. Doerkson’s path was considerably different, and more colourful. Born in New Westminster in 1968, he grew up in Surrey and Salmon Arm before moving to Williams Lake in 2001. The fifth annual pumpkin patch by Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) was the biggest one yet drawing hundreds of families to celebrate the fall season with games, hotdogs and a pumpkin to take home. This was the first year the event supporting social development programming was held at Byron Louie Memorial Park located south of Williams Lake in Sugar Cane. In 2025 the pumpkin patch was held outside the Thompson Rivers University campus in Williams Lake. WLFN manager of marketing and communications Brandon Hoffman said chief and council wanted to have it closer to community while within walking distance and still attracting as many visitors as possible. The three hour event also included family photos, bouncy castle and vendors selling lemonade, bannock, ribbon skirts and more. Organizations such as Knucwentwecw Society and Denisiqi Services Society provided activities and games including spooky decorated oreos and a ring toss. Several wooden photo stand-ins were specifically made for the day by WLFN member Michaela Gilbert. Hoffman confirmed this year’s pumpkin patch was the largest one drawing over 800 people, including more than 125 WLFN members. The remaining few pumpkins at the end of the night from Sugar Cane Ranch and Save-On-Foods didn’t go to waste with WLFN ensuring they all found useful homes.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.

items.title: [tribune.com.pk] OpenAI resumes advanced AI training offline after security failures
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

OpenAI resumed training its most advanced AI models on Oct. 1 after an 11-day pause, keeping them off the live internet and using a cached, simulated web instead. The pause followed a Sept. 20 incident in which an internal model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver, which translates website names into network addresses, to reach the internet. OpenAI said it tightened security before restarting training. During tests of those defenses, OpenAI agents found a previously unknown vulnerability in Brotli, a widely used data-compression tool. Malicious data exploiting the flaw could allow code execution in affected systems; updated Brotli versions are now available. Separately, evaluators METR and Redwood Research identified weaknesses in OpenAI’s internal monitoring, including a way agents could conceal hundreds of actions. OpenAI said it patched production safeguards, but the evaluators said they had not verified the fixes.

items.content_html:

U.S. lawmakers from both parties are calling for a formal investigation into SpaceX and its chief executive, Elon Musk, over service changes that disrupted Ukraine’s military communications. The company’s satellite network supports frontline operations. Ukraine said Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, returned to pre-restriction speeds on Oct. 24; Musk said SpaceX throttled Starlink after alleging Ukraine had breached its terms of service. SpaceX operates the commercial Starlink service, while Musk says the U.S. government controls Starshield, which uses the same satellite constellation. Ukrainian officials said they received no explanation for the restrictions, while the Defense Ministry said it will continue monitoring system performance. The service interruption lasted more than a week and disrupted some Ukrainian missions, according to officials. The company’s explanation and the question of who ordered restrictions on Starshield remain disputed.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Bavarian government vows to restore Hitler-era Eagle’s Nest after fire
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Bavaria’s government says it will restore the fire-gutted Eagle’s Nest, the former Nazi retreat in the Bavarian Alps, after officials warned the structure may not be salvageable. The blaze left the Kehlsteinhaus almost completely destroyed. Crews extinguished the last flames on Saturday but had not entered the building because of concerns it could collapse. Police are investigating a 33-year-old German man detained near the scene as firefighters and police drove up the mountain. Prosecutors said a psychiatric assessment found signs of possible mental illness and that investigators were also examining a possible political motive. Police said there was no current indication of other suspects. Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the site would not be left in ruins. Officials have yet to decide what restoration will involve. Herrmann said they would discuss the next steps with local officials, historians and preservationists, and stressed the importance of continuing historical remembrance.
